name: Y+
seoDesc: Y+: work out freestream velocity (Uf) from the density and the dynamic viscosity. A free physics calculator with the formula, units and a worked example.
summary: Give the Y+ calculator the density, the dynamic viscosity, the length of boundary layer and the dimensionless distance and it returns freestream velocity (Uf). It is built for a lab report, a problem set or a sanity check on a physical situation. Every field is labelled the way you would say it out loud, so you can usually fill the form from memory and only look up the numbers you genuinely do not know.

sections.title: How does the Y+ calculator work?
sections.html:
The Y+ calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports freestream velocity (Uf) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the skin friction coefficient approximation); then you type in the density (ρ), the dynamic viscosity (μ), the length of boundary layer (L) and the dimensionless distance (y+).

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Y+ calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Freestream velocity (Uf)=dynamic viscosity (μ) × reynold's number (Re) ÷ (density (ρ) × length of boundary layer (L))
Skin friction coefficient (Cf)=(reynold's number (Re), skin friction coefficient approximation)
Shear stress (𝜏w)=((1 ÷ 2) × density (ρ) × (freestream velocity (Uf) ^ 2) × (reynold's number (Re), skin friction coefficient approximation))
Friction velocity (u)=(the square root of (((1 ÷ 2) × density (ρ) × (freestream velocity (Uf) ^ 2) × (reynold's number (Re), skin friction coefficient approximation)) ÷ density (ρ)))
Wall distance (y)=(dynamic viscosity (μ) × dimensionless distance (y+) ÷ (density (ρ) × (the square root of (((1 ÷ 2) × density (ρ) × (freestream velocity (Uf) ^ 2) × (reynold's number (Re), skin friction coefficient approximation)) ÷ density (ρ)))))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Units are handled by conversion rather than by convention. Whatever chip you choose, the number is turned into a single base unit before the calculation and rendered back afterwards, so a form filled with a mixture of systems still gives the right answer.

  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Density, opening in kilograms per cubic meter
  • Pressure, opening in millipascals
  • Length, opening in meters
  • Pressure, opening in pascals
  • Speed, opening in meters per second
  • Length, opening in millimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Y+ calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Solving a problem set where the algebra is more interesting than the arithmetic
  • Writing up a lab result and needing a quick cross-check
  • Testing whether an answer is physically plausible before you trust it
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the density, the dynamic viscosity and the length of boundary layer — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Change one input at a time when you are exploring. Two simultaneous changes make it impossible to tell which one moved the result.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

faq.q: What does the Y+ calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns freestream velocity (Uf), derived from the density, the dynamic viscosity and the length of boundary layer. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Y+ calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the density, the dynamic viscosity, the length of boundary layer and the dimensionless distance, which is 6 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter freestream velocity (Uf) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Freestream velocity (Uf) opens in meters per second and the chip beside it offers 25 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There is one choice to make (1 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

faq.q: Is the Y+ calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
